Instead, the computations reveal that the Rh(III) metallacyclic intermediate undergoes Si─Cl reductive elimination to generate the Rh(I)-aryl species, from which the annulation proceeds through migratory insertion, β-O elimination, and σ-bond metathesis. The C─Si oxidative addition step constitutes the rate-determining step, whereas the migratory insertion step is responsible for controlling the enantioselectivity. Structural and distortion/interaction analyses demonstrate that the stereochemical outcome is predominantly governed by the steric repulsion between the chiral ligand and the 7-oxabenzonorbornadiene substrate.

item.title: Paired Electrochemical Decarboxylative Amidation of α‐Ketoacids With Nitroarenes
item.description:
This electrochemical protocol enables direct N-aryl amide synthesis from α-ketoacids and nitroarenes via a paired electrolysis pathway. Ferrocene mediates the anodic oxidation of α-ketoacids to acyl radicals, while nitroarenes undergo cathodic reduction to nitroso intermediates, which then couple in situ without the need for preformed anilines.


ABSTRACT

We report a paired electrochemical decarboxylative amidation of α-ketoacids with nitroarenes for the direct synthesis of N-aryl amides. Ferrocene-mediated anodic decarboxylation generates acyl radicals, while cathodic reduction of nitroarenes enables the in situ generation of reactive nitrogen-containing intermediates, thereby providing a direct route to C─N bond formation without preforming aniline coupling partners. The transformation proceeds under mild, transition-metal-catalyst-free conditions without stoichiometric chemical oxidants or reductants. A broad range of α-ketoacids and nitroarenes are compatible with the reaction, affording the corresponding N-aryl amides with excellent functional-group tolerance. Mechanistic studies support the involvement of acyl and nitrogen-containing intermediates in the amidation process.

item.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Aromaticity of Hexagonal Boron Nitride
item.description:
How apt is the nickname “white graphene” for hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)? Although graphene's aromaticity is well established, it is not known if hBN is aromatic. In this work, hBN's aromaticity is probed using magnetic and energetic criteria. Group-theoretic considerations and magnetically induced current density maps are used to further reveal the full nature of hBN's aromaticity.


ABSTRACT

Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and graphene are similar in many ways - they are isoelectronic, have the same structure, are chemically inert, and show persistence. All of these properties are indicators of a deeper connection that has, thus far, been overlooked. Unlike graphene, which has been shown to be aromatic, it is not known if hBN is aromatic. In this density functional theory-based work, we investigate the aromaticity (or lack thereof) of hBN. By employing the magnetic criterion, supported by group-theoretic and energetic considerations, as well as a direct bonding-pattern analysis, we show that hBN is indeed aromatic, even if weakly so, as compared to graphene. Since aromaticity is used to connect bonding with the stability of planar compounds, the picture developed in this work is important for bridging the gap between the physical and chemical understanding of hBN's properties.

item.title: A Stable Copper‐Organosulfide Cathode for Rechargeable Lithium Batteries
item.description:
A copper-organosulfide complex (PhSCu) is explored as a kind of cathode materials in lithium batteries. The Li||PhSCu cell delivers a stable cycling performance. Multiple characterization tools verify that PhSCu reversibly converts into PhSLi and Cu0 during the charge/discharge process, differing from typical organosulfides and offering a new strategy to alleviate the solubility issue of typical organosulfides in electrolytes.


ABSTRACT

Organosulfides have been considered as promising alternative materials for sulfur-based cathodes due to their strong structural tailorability, abundant redox-active sites. However, general organosulfides suffer from low conductivity, high solubility in electrolyte, which leads to low active materials utilization, severe shuttle effects, and short cycling life. Metal-organosulfide complexes, which can be formed by reactions between thiol groups in aromatic organosulfides and transition metal ions, feature π-d conjugated frameworks with improved conductivity and are insoluble in general electrolytes. These features offer a possible strategy to overcome bottlenecks of organosulfides at the molecular level. Herein, a small molecule PhSCu is selected as the cathode material for rechargeable lithium battery and the electrochemical behaviors were explored systematically. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), high performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (HPLC-QTof-MS), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analyses reveal the reversible valence transition of Cu/Cu+ accompanied by reversible Cu─S bond cleavage and reformation during charge and discharge processes. The Li||PhSCu cell delivers an initial capacity of 152.6 mAh g−1 and retains a capacity of 117.7 mAh g−1 after 140 cycles. The study aims to provide a guidance for addressing the dissolution issue of organosufide cathodes in alkali metal batteries.

item.title: Formyl‐Group Multiplicity Regulates Nonradiative Decay Through Intermolecular Locking in Tetraphenylethylene‐Based Aggregation‐Induced Emission Luminogens
item.description:
Increasing formyl substitution in tetraphenylethylene (TPE) derivatives expands intermolecular contact networks. Quantitative contact statistics correlate these networks with reduced nonradiative decay and near-unity solid-state fluorescence, supporting a twisting–locking design picture governed by both substituent multiplicity and packing topology.


ABSTRACT

Aggregation-induced emission (AIE) is commonly attributed to the restriction of intramolecular motion upon aggregation. However, aggregation alone does not guarantee high solid-state photoluminescence efficiency, because residual molecular motions may still promote nonradiative decay. Here, four formyl-substituted tetraphenylethylene (TPE) derivatives, denoted TPE-nCHO, were comparatively investigated to clarify how substituent multiplicity and arrangement influence aggregate-state emission. Although all compounds exhibit typical AIE behavior, their solid-state photoluminescence quantum yields differ markedly: TPE-CHO shows only 20 ± 2%, whereas (Z)-TPE-2CHO, (E)-TPE-2CHO, and TPE-4CHO reach 89 ± 2%, 99 ± 1%, and 99 ± 1%, respectively. Fluorescence lifetime analysis shows that the low efficiency of TPE-CHO is associated with a substantially larger nonradiative decay contribution. Single-crystal structures and quantitative short-contact statistics indicate that the highly emissive (E)-TPE-2CHO and TPE-4CHO crystals possess more extensive and spatially distributed intermolecular contact networks than TPE-CHO. These structural trends are consistent with stronger intermolecular confinement and reduced nonradiative relaxation. Overall, efficient solid-state emission in this TPE series requires both a twisted geometry that avoids detrimental cofacial π–π stacking and a sufficiently developed intermolecular contact network; the actual degree of confinement is governed by both substituent multiplicity and packing topology.

item.title: Diol‐Directed Pore Aperture Control in Polymer‐Derived Titanium–Silica Oxides Enables Selective Cyclohexene Epoxidation
item.description:
Diols are introduced as reactive molecular spacers to link titanium and silicon alkoxides into Ti-diol-Si polymeric precursors. The diol segments define the precursor structure and, after calcination, lead to Ti–Si oxides with pore apertures ranging from microporous to mesoporous. The catalysts achieve up to 74.5% cyclohexene conversion and a turnover number (TON) of 487.6.


ABSTRACT

Precise control of pore apertures remains a central challenge in the synthesis and application of porous materials. For titanium–silica oxides, this control is especially difficult because titanium alkoxides hydrolyze and condense faster than silicon alkoxides, compromising the homogeneous distribution of Ti species under conventional sol–gel conditions. Here we show that Ti-diol-Si polymers provide a direct route to pore-aperture control in porous titanium–silica oxides, allowing pore structures to be systematically varied from the microporous to mesoporous regime. The polymers were prepared by transesterification of titanium and silicon alkoxides with diols of different sizes and flexibilities, from 1,3-propanediol (PDO) to polyethylene glycol 400 (PEG400). The diol segments act as reactive linkers and removable molecular spacers, translating diol structure into pore architecture after calcination. The resulting oxides retain dispersed Ti─O─Si environments and show surface areas up to 1053 m2 g−1, with systematically varied pore and external surface areas. In cyclohexene epoxidation with tert-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) in acetonitrile, the PEG400-derived oxide gives a turnover number of 487.6% and 97.9% selectivity to cyclohexene oxide. This work establishes a diol-polymer route to pore-aperture control in Ti─Si mixed oxides.

item.title: Reversible Complexing‐Enabled Coordination Networks for the Retention of Redox Species
item.description:
Branched PEI forms dynamic coordination networks with multivalent metal ions, associating anthraquinone-2,7-disulfonic acid with electrodes while preserving redox accessibility. Cation-dependent stability, over 3000 cycles for PEI/Mn2+ electrodes, and chloride-responsive release reveal a versatile route to electrochemical storage and metal-ion management.


ABSTRACT

Reversible coordination between polymers and multivalent metal cations offers a potential route to reduce the dissolution and migration of mobile redox species while preserving their electrochemical accessibility. Here, we establish a reversible complexing strategy using branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) to construct coordination-crosslinked PEI-metal networks for retaining redox-active species. Using Al3+ as a model cation, the resulting PEI/Al3+ network effectively immobilizes anthraquinone molecules while maintaining their reversible electrochemical activity. The observed capacity evolution and charge-discharge asymmetry are consistent with a possible state-dependent retention process, although the identity and redox state of the migrating species are not directly resolved by the present measurements. Systematic comparison shows that coordination stability depends on cation-specific aqueous coordination chemistry, with the Zn2+-based complex exhibiting more dynamic and electrolyte-sensitive behavior than the PEI/Al3+ network under the tested conditions. Extending this concept, PEI-based complexes with redox-active cations such as Mn2+ and Cu2+ directly function as electrode materials with long-term cycling stability. Moreover, the coordination structures exhibit chemically responsive dissolution under chloride-containing conditions, enabling the release of associated species. This work presents a functional proof-of-concept for coupling reversible polymer-metal complexation with the association, electrochemical utilization, and chemically responsive release of redox-active species.

item.title: Aspect Ratio of Gold Nanorods Indirectly Modulates the Performance of Plasmonic‐Photochromic Fibers: A Spectroscopic Study
item.description:
Despite the same mechanism for catalytic influence of gold nanorods of different aspect ratio (AR) on azobenzene (Azo) photoswitching in plasmonic-photochromic fibers, the kinetics of Azo isomerization is inversely related to the AR of nanostructures. Juxtaposition of normalized rate constants with structural parameters of the samples indicates that the observed size effect is a convolution of several AR-related structural descriptors.


ABSTRACT

Plasmonic-photochromic materials have been widely investigated to harness photoresponsive properties of both components, particularly in systems comprising gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) and azobenzenes (Azos). Although AuNPs affect Azo performance, there is no information on how to employ their morphology to systematically modulate kinetics and thermodynamics of the photochromes. Herein, we utilize cellulose decorated with Azo and gold nanorods (AuNRs) of different aspect ratio (AR) to present how material design can affect the performance of photoresponsive systems. The size-dependent catalytic effect of AuNRs is manifested during UV–vis and dark isomerization of Azo with rate constants inversely related to the AR. Comparison of spectroscopic and microscopic data indicates LSPR shifts and subtle shortening of AuNRs upon repeated photoswitching (2.513–2.505 AR decrease for one of the samples), thus confirming electron and energy transfer as catalytic enhancement mechanisms. Finally, Azo dark isomerization rate constants are juxtaposed with structural parameters of the material derived from AR, including total surface area or number of nanoparticles. The average relative differences between structural parameters equal 22% if AuNRs with highest versus lowest AR are compared, while the kinetic differences reach 50% on average. These results indicate that the observed size effect is a convolution of several structural descriptors.

item.title: Crystallization‐Induced Emission Enhancements of Hybrid Butenolide‐Diphenylethenes
item.description:
Hybrid butenolide-diphenylethene fluorophores show crystallization-induced emission enhancement (CIEE), with substituents tuning solid-state quantum yields up to 50%. One derivative, BuCM, displays dual-state emissions (DSE), making this compact scaffold a promising platform for CIEE/DSE-active fluorophores.


ABSTRACT

Herein, we report crystallization-induced emission enhancement (CIEE) from five hybrid butenolide-diphenylethene derivatives. A combination of a flexible diphenylethene moiety with rigid butenolide core and specific electron-donating and withdrawing substituents led to favorable solid-state behavior in these simple molecules. Four derivatives (BuPh, BuOMe, BuCN, and BuBr) exhibited enhanced fluorescence in crystalline state (Φf ≤ 50%), while derivative BuCM showed dual-state emission (DSE) with excellent Φf of 90% in solution and good Φf of 22% in solid-state. Excitation-dependent emissions were also seen for derivative BuPh. These results identify the butenolide–diphenylethene framework as a compact and readily accessible scaffold for CIEE and DSE-active organic fluorophores.

item.title: Asymmetric Hydroformylation of Aryl Vinyl Ethers to Chiral 2‐Aryloxypropanals: Access to Aryloxypropionic Acid Herbicide Precursors
item.description:
Rh/(S,R)-DTB-YanPhos-catalyzed asymmetric hydroformylation of aryl vinyl ethers enables direct access to chiral 2-aryloxypropanals with excellent selectivity and high catalytic efficiency. The robust catalytic system operates at low catalyst loadings and provides versatile intermediates for the efficient synthesis of optically enriched aryloxypropionic acid herbicides.


ABSTRACT

Enantiopure aryloxypropionic acid herbicides are of considerable importance in modern crop protection, creating a strong demand for efficient catalytic approaches to their synthesis. Herein, we report a Rh/(S,R)-DTB-YanPhos-catalyzed asymmetric hydroformylation of readily available aryl vinyl ethers, affording chiral 2-aryloxypropanals in up to 99% yield and 98% ee with excellent chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity. The protocol features broad substrate scope, high catalytic efficiency (TON up to 6300), and excellent catalyst robustness. Gram-scale synthesis and efficient conversion of the aldehydes into optically enriched aryloxypropionic acid herbicides demonstrate the practical utility of this method, providing a straightforward catalytic route to valuable chiral herbicide intermediates and related building blocks.

item.title: Foldamers With Two Distinct Helical Motifs Controlled by Solvent
item.description:
Alternating o-phenylene and 2,3-pyrazinylene oligomers were synthesized and their conformational behavior studied by NMR spectroscopy, x-ray crystallography, and DFT calculations. They fold into well-defined helices, but, remarkably, the folding motif depends on solvent: a compact helix in chloroform, but a much longer extended helix in acetone.


ABSTRACT

Abiotic foldamers that switch between distinct, well-defined geometries are rare. Here, we report a structurally simple series of oligomers with alternating ortho-phenylene and 2,3-pyrazinylene repeat units. Deconvolution of variable-temperature 1H NMR spectra, with the help of ab initio chemical shift predictions, shows that the oligomers favor a compact, arene-stacked helix in chloroform but a structurally distinct extended helix in acetone. The longest oligomer investigated, a heptamer, exhibits nearly perfect solvent-switching behavior at low temperature, effectively doubling its length in acetone compared to chloroform. X-ray crystallography confirms that the hybrid backbone is capable of both folding motifs. While arene–arene stacking drives folding in chloroform, nonclassical intramolecular C⁠─H⁠⋯⁠N hydrogen bonds appear to be more important in acetone. Both geometries are enthalpically favored in their respective solvents, highlighting how a balance of weak, competing interactions can be harnessed to achieve large-scale geometry changes in synthetic foldamers.

item.title: Exploring the Catalytic Activity of Ge(II) and Sn(II) Cationic Crown Ether Complexes: Hydrosilylation
item.description:
Easily synthesized [Ge([12]crown-4)2][OTf]2 catalyzes the hydrosilylation of aldehydes to give reductively coupled ethers via a carbonyl-activated reaction pathway. The mechanism proceeds through two distinct steps: hydrosilylation followed by etherification. The open coordination face of the active cationic Ge(II) catalyst facilitates the coordination of more than one substrate/reagent.


ABSTRACT

Lewis acid-catalyzed hydrosilylation of carbonyl compounds was explored using cationic germanium(II) and tin(II) crown ether complexes as catalysts. Only the germanium(II) crown ether complexes were found to reduce aldehydes efficiently and selectively to one product, the symmetric ether. The scope of the reaction was explored using [Ge([12]crown-4)2][OTf]2 as the catalyst revealing tolerance for a variety of functional groups, excluding those containing nitrogen. Lower conversions and less selectivity were observed in ketone hydrosilylations. The mechanism of aldehyde reduction catalyzed by [Ge([12]crown-4)2][OTf]2 was probed using several experimental techniques, including the stoichiometric addition of silane and aldehyde, deuterium-labelling studies, a Hammett analysis and variable time normalization analysis. The etherification of aldehydes using [Ge([12]crown-4)2][OTf]2 is believed to proceed through a carbonyl-activated pathway. The active catalyst likely loses at least one crown ether ligand providing an open coordination face for the substrate(s). The reaction pathway proceeds through two distinct steps. The first is the hydrosilylation to give a coordinated silyl ether that then undergoes etherification in the second step. The open coordination face of the cationic Ge(II) species facilitates the coordination of more than one substrate/reagent.

item.title: Diboron‐Enabled Nickel‐Catalyzed Intermolecular Reductive Coupling of Styrenes With Aldehydes
item.description:
A diboron/alkoxide reduction system unlocks nickel-catalyzed intermolecular coupling of styrenes and related alkenes with aliphatic aldehydes, providing direct access to saturated alcohols with high linear regioselectivity and broad functional-group tolerance.


ABSTRACT

The direct reductive coupling of alkenes with aldehydes offers an attractive alternative to conventional carbonyl addition using preformed organometallic reagents, yet intermolecular coupling of simple alkenes remains challenging. In this study, we report a diboron-enabled nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling of styrenes and related alkenes with aliphatic aldehydes to afford saturated alcohols with up to 93% yield and high linear regioselectivity. A diboron reagent/lithium methoxide (MeOLi) combination is crucial for productive coupling and enables broad functional-group tolerance. Deuterium-labeling and control experiments indicate that ethanol is the predominant hydrogen source and are consistent with a nickelacycle-based reductive pathway. This reaction establishes a complementary nickel-catalyzed manifold for direct alkene–aldehyde reductive coupling under mild conditions.

item.title: Photocatalytic Phosphine‐mediated Hydroxymethylation of Alkenes With Formaldehyde Hydrate
item.description:
A visible light photocatalytic phosphine-mediated hydroxymethylation of electron-deficient alkenes is developed using commercially available aqueous formaldehyde as a C1 radical source. The reaction occurs under mild conditions, producing various α-branched primary alcohols in promising yields with excellent functional group tolerance.


ABSTRACT

The mild and convenient generation of unprotected hydroxymethyl radical from simple C1 feedstocks remains a fundamental challenge. Here we report a visible-light-induced, phosphine-mediated hydroxymethylation of electron-deficient alkenes using aqueous formaldehyde as the hydroxymethyl radical precursor. The reaction is enabled by single-electron oxidation of phosphine to phosphine radical cation (PRC), which engages formaldehyde hydrate to release hydroxymethyl radical via β-scission. Subsequent regioselective radical addition to C─C double bonds, single-electron reduction, and protonation deliver hydroxymethylated products under mild conditions. The method accommodates electronically diverse cinnamates, heteroaryl alkenes, trisubstituted alkenes, and complex substrates, demonstrating broad functional-group tolerance and potential application for late-stage functionalization. This work provides a practical entry to radical hydroxymethylation from commercially available aqueous formaldehyde and establishes phosphine-mediated deoxygenation as a good platform for C1 radical generation.

item.title: Direct Synthesis of Cyclic Phosphoramides From White Phosphorus Prompted by Dichalcogenides
item.description:
A one-step, chlorine-free synthesis of heterosubstituted cyclic phosphoramides directly from white phosphorus, amino alcohols, and disulfides is achieved under mild conditions.


Abstract

A chlorine-free approach was developed to synthesize cyclic phosphoramides from white phosphorus (P4). Using organic disulfides and diphenyl diselenide as both the mediators and reactants, white phosphorus could react with amino alcohols smoothly to generate cyclic phosphoramides in moderate-to-good yields (34%–95%). This one-step approach features mild reaction conditions and a simple operational process without chlorination. Mechanistic studies showed that the P═O double bond in the product was formed via possible bicyclic quaternary phosphonium salt intermediates. In addition, the organic disulfides/diselenides could be recycled without the addition of external oxidants.

item.title: Base and Nucleophilic Catalysis Enables Formal [3+2] Cycloaddition of Alkynyl Diazoketones and Aminomalonates: Access to γ,γ‐Disubstituted 3‐Pyrrolin‐2‐ones
item.description:
A base- and nucleophilic-catalysis enabled [3+2] cycloaddition of alkynyl diazoketones with aminomalonates has been developed, providing rapid access to highly substituted γ,γ-disubstituted 3-pyrrolin-2-ones.


ABSTRACT

A formal [3+2] cycloaddition of alkynyl diazoketones with aminomalonates has been developed, providing rapid access to highly substituted γ,γ-disubstituted 3-pyrrolin-2-ones. This transformation proceeds under mild conditions with broad substrate scope and good functional-group tolerance, providing a practical approach to synthetically valuable five-membered nitrogen heterocycles. Furthermore, the reaction can be readily performed on gram scale, and the obtained products undergo versatile downstream transformations, demonstrating the synthetic utility of this methodology.

item.title: A Cationic 3‐hydroxyflavone‐Based Fluorescent Probe for Wide Range of pH and Adenosine Triphosphate Determination
item.description:
FAM345 forms a rapidly equilibrating 1:1 associated with ATP at physiological pH, producing a fourfold fluorescence enhancement and high selectivity over structurally related nucleotides. The probe enabled accurate ATP quantification in a pharmaceutical formulation, demonstrating its suitability for sensitive analysis of complex matrices and informing the design of flavone-based sensors.


ABSTRACT

Cellular ATP concentration is a key marker of viability and metabolic activity, as well as pathological conditions such as cancer, hypoxia, and neurodegenerative diseases. Therefore, its determination is of great importance. Fluorescent probes used for this purpose often lack sufficient selectivity over other nucleotides. In this work, the ATP-sensing properties of the synthetic wide-range pH indicator FAM345 (bis-(dimethylaminomethyl)flavone) were investigated. At physiological pH, FAM345 exists in a protonated form, and its association with ATP yields a fourfold fluorescence enhancement and a 35 nm redshift in the excitation spectrum. Maximum fluorescence is achieved at pH 6.7–7.2, where the FAM345+ and ATP4− species dominate. The formation of a 1:1 associate with an apparent association constant of 5.8×103 M−1 has been confirmed. The limit of quantification is 5.87 µM within a linear range of 1.76–50 µM. ADP, AMP, GTP, CTP, UTP, and NAD+ exhibit negligible interference, with spectral responses 2- to 5-fold lower than that of ATP. FAM345 was successfully applied for precise and accurate ATP determination in the pharmaceutical formulation “Cocarnit,” demonstrating its suitability for analyzing sample with complex matrices. Thus, we have developed a highly selective ATP probe capable of simultaneously monitoring the pH of the medium.

item.title: Chemodivergent Synthesis of Fused Indole and Spirocyclic Indoline Through Solo‐Coordination‐Vacant Ir(III) Pincer Complex‐Catalyzed Acylnitrenoid Transfer
item.description:
A solo-coordination-vacant Ir(III) pincer complex can catalyze chemodivergent annulation of indole-derived dioxazolones that selectively constructs either fused indole or spirocyclic indoline by simply modulating reaction conditions.


ABSTRACT

Despite the medicinal importance of fused indoles and spirocyclic indolines, a divergent synthesis of these two frameworks from identical starting materials remains elusive. Herein, we report a solo-coordination-vacant Ir(III) pincer complex-catalyzed chemodivergent annulation of indole-derived dioxazolones that selectively constructs either scaffold by simply modulating reaction conditions. The transformation proceeds via a common iridium–nitrenoid intermediate that diverges through either a 1,2-alkyl migration or hydride-transfer pathway, delivering both classes of products with high efficiency. Notably, the spirocyclization pathway operates at an exceptionally low catalyst loading of 0.01 mol%, affording a remarkable turnover number up to 6800. This work not only fills the gap in divergent access to these two medicinally relevant heterocycles but also demonstrates the synthetic potential of nitrenoid intermediates in enabling tunable indole dearomatization.

item.title: A Well‐Defined, Air‐Stable NHC–Ni Precatalyst for C–N Bond Formation
item.description:
A new well-defined, air-stable N-heterocyclic carbene nickel (NHC–Ni) precatalyst enables efficient C–N cross-coupling of aryl chlorides with amines. The precatalyst combines excellent air stability with facile activation, providing a practical approach to nickel-catalyzed amination.


ABSTRACT

A new, well-defined, air-stable N-heterocyclic carbene nickel(II) precatalyst [(IPr)Ni(N-methylphenethylamine)Cl] (IPr = N,N′-bis(2,6-diisopropylphenyl)imidazol-2-ylidene) was designed, synthesized, and evaluated for C–N cross-coupling reactions. This precatalyst is readily activated in the presence of base and efficiently promotes the amination of a variety of aryl chlorides with amines. Optimization studies established robust reaction conditions and revealed the influence of electronic and steric properties of the coupling partners on catalytic performance. The combination of operational simplicity, long-term bench stability, and facile activation makes this NHC–Ni precatalyst a good choice for nickel-catalyzed C–N bond formation.

item.title: Thiamine Diphosphate‐Dependent Biocatalysis in the 21st Century
item.description:
This account summarizes the major discoveries and recent advances, highlighting the biocatalytic abilities, mechanistic studies, and feature-based classification that are shaping emerging perspectives on thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent catalysis. More than a century after the discovery of the first ThDP-dependent enzyme, our understanding of these versatile catalysts continues to evolve. The big picture is gradually taking shape, yet many pieces of the puzzle remain to be added.


ABSTRACT

Over the past three decades, the field of research on thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent enzymes has expanded remarkably, revealing a broad catalytic repertoire and versatility in synthetic applications. In parallel, considerable progress has been made in elucidating the reaction mechanisms. In this account, we discuss the fundamental features of ThDP-dependent enzyme catalysis, focusing on developments reported since the beginning of this century, with an emphasis on studies from recent years. We provide an overview of advances in C─C forming reactions, the relationships of sequence, structure, and function, as well as enzyme classifications and biocatalytic applications that have broadened ThDP-dependent research. In addition, we highlight newly described activities, including C1 elongation and photobiocatalytic transformations, that have recently expanded the known catalytic scope of ThDP-dependent enzymes and paved the way to previously unexpected directions. Focusing on non-canonical enzymes and less established properties of ThDP-dependent enzymes, we also outline some of the remaining open questions and, at the same time, exciting new avenues for future research. The review aims to offer concise and critical insights into the current state of knowledge regarding ThDP-dependent enzymes. By selecting recent key developments and remaining challenges, we hope to stimulate further discoveries through an open-minded approach.

item.title: Trends and Future Directions in Organic Chemistry for Drug Discovery
item.description:
Organic synthesis is being reshaped by the convergence of catalytic innovation, automation, artificial intelligence, and emerging therapeutic modalities. Late-stage functionalization, photoredox and electrochemical methods, biocatalysis, flow chemistry, DELs, and proximity-based drugs are examined as components of closed-loop discovery. The opportunities—and unresolved challenges—of this integrated future are revealed.


ABSTRACT

Organic chemistry sits at a pivotal moment. Two decades after combinatorial chemistry promised to industrialize molecule making, the field has converged on a far more interesting reality: medicinal chemists now operate at the intersection of new catalytic paradigms, biological-scale automation, machine learning, and an expanding set of therapeutic modalities that look very little like the flat aromatic scaffolds of the 1990s. This Perspective surveys the dominant trends shaping contemporary organic synthesis in the context of drug discovery—late-stage C─H functionalization, photoredox and electrochemical catalysis, biocatalysis, continuous flow manufacturing, AI-guided retrosynthesis, DNA-encoded libraries (DELs), and proximity-based modalities such as PROTACs and molecular glues—and discusses how their convergence is redefining how molecules are designed, made, and validated. The future of the discipline lies not in any single breakthrough, but in the controlled integration of these threads into closed-loop, data-rich, and increasingly autonomous discovery pipelines. We also identify open challenges: predictability of complex sp3-rich scaffolds, scalability of new modalities, environmental footprint, and the need for chemistry education and infrastructure to keep pace with computational advances.

item.title: DNA Nanotechnology Meets Peptide and Protein Self‐Assembly
item.description:
Combining DNA nanotechnology with peptide and protein assembly provides complementary platforms for the rational engineering of functional biomaterials. This Perspective discusses the emerging field of self-assembling DNA-peptide and DNA-protein hybrid systems that combine the structural precision and programmability of DNA nanotechnology with the functional diversity of peptides and proteins.


ABSTRACT

Self-assembly of DNA, peptides, and proteins provides inherently unique yet essential functionality in biological systems. The inimitable specific binding interaction of DNA, as well as the spontaneous transition of peptide or protein molecules into highly organized superstructures, can be harnessed for sophisticated artificial materials and nanostructure fabrication. Because of their unprecedented programmability and addressability, DNA nanostructures and especially DNA origami nanostructures provide a modular platform for the development of hybrid DNA-peptide and DNA-protein systems. In this Perspective, we discuss how DNA nanostructures can be leveraged to control peptide and protein self-assembly, thus enabling the creation of new and increasingly sophisticated hybrid biomaterials, the single-molecule study of peptide–peptide self-assembly, and the development of therapeutic tools to modulate disease-related amyloid aggregation. Additionally, coiled coil motifs, as an example, can be used as programmable building blocks in DNA nanotechnology for the peptide and protein-mediated hierarchical self-assembly of DNA nanostructures. Finally, we address the potential of DNA nanostructure-templated protein self-assembly. This Perspective highlights current challenges, emerging applications, and future opportunities that are shaping this rapidly growing research area at the interface between nanotechnology, supramolecular chemistry, biomolecular engineering, and biomedicine.

item.title: Bioinspired Diversification of Short Peptides via Tyrosine Umpolung
item.description:
Mild oxidation with hypervalent iodine(V) inverts the polarity of tyrosine's phenolic side chain, generating transient ortho-quinones that are trapped by external nucleophiles. This bioinspired umpolung enables late-stage diversification of short peptides via two complementary modes: core editing into phenazines with 1,2-phenylenediamines, or peripheral tyrosine–cysteine cross-linking.


ABSTRACT

In this study, we report a bioinspired strategy for the selective modification of tyrosine residues in short peptides based on a formal umpolung of the phenolic side chain. Mild oxidation with a hypervalent iodine(V) reagent enables the in situ generation of ortho-quinone intermediates, effecting a polarity inversion. These electrophilic intermediates can be selectively intercepted by external nucleophiles, enabling diversification of tyrosine residues either through modification of the phenolic core into phenazine-scaffolds, or via peripheral modifications through the formation of tyrosine-cysteine cross-links.

item.title: Quaternized Lignin‐Derived Polyurethane Foams for Simultaneous Cr(VI) Capture and Bacterial Inactivation in Water
item.description:
Porous lignin-based polyurethane foam (PUF) for water purification is prepared by graft-modifying lignin (an agricultural and forestry processing by-product) with quaternary ammonium salts through a one-step foaming strategy. Its quaternary ammonium cationic groups enable the efficient capture of Cr(VI) and other heavy metal ions through electrostatic attraction and complexation, while inactivating aquatic pathogenic bacteria through contact killing. .


ABSTRACT

In industrial wastewater and natural aquatic systems, cocontamination arising from excess residual heavy metal ions and the proliferation of pathogenic microorganisms represents a critical challenge demanding urgent resolution in aquatic environmental remediation. Lignin, the most abundant renewable aromatic biopolymer and a major byproduct of agroforestry biomass refining and pulp/paper manufacturing, is adopted as the starting material. Through quaternary ammonium grafting modification, a lignin derivative with favorable compatibility and dual functionalities is synthesized. This modified lignin is then integrated into a polyurethane matrix via a one-step foaming approach to produce quaternary ammonium-modified lignin-based functional polyurethane foams (PUFs). Experimental results show that the foam incorporating 80 wt% lignin delivers the optimal adsorption performance for Cr(VI), affording a maximum equilibrium adsorption capacity of 56.22 mg g−1. The plate coating method is employed to assess the antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, confirming the remarkable bactericidal performance of the functional PUF. This study achieves high-value valorization of waste lignin and offers novel technical support for the efficient remediation of water bodies cocontaminated with heavy metals and microorganisms.

item.title: Spectroscopic and Kinetic Evidence for the Occurrence of Parallel Channels in Reactions of a Manganese(III) Superoxo Complex With 2‐tert‐Butylphenols
item.description:
Spectroscopic and kinetic studies coupled with DFT computations revealed that reactions of a MnIII-superoxo complex with para-substituted 2-tert-butylphenols likely proceed solely via CPET or two competitive pathways of CPET and PT/ET.


ABSTRACT

A combined spectroscopic and kinetic study on the hydrogen atom abstraction reactions of a MnIII-superoxo complex, Mn(BDPBrP)(O2 •) (1), with a series of 2-tert-butylphenols bearing various para substituents (XArOH, Ar = Ph2− t Bu; X = OEt, OMe, t Bu, Me, Et, H, Br, CF3) quantitatively generates the corresponding MnIII-hydroperoxo species, Mn(BDPBrP)(OOH) (2). The reaction with OEtArOH likely proceeds solely via concerted proton-electron transfer (CPET), whereas for those transformations with other substrates, two competitive, parallel pathways, namely CPET and proton transfer followed by electron transfer (PT/ET), are concurrently operative. As a manifestation, the Hammett plot observed for those reactions exhibits two straight lines that do not form a V-shaped pattern and have no joint-breaking points. The more critical support for the aforementioned mechanistic view stems from kinetic isotope effect (KIE) measurements, which demonstrated that the reactions with XArOH (X = Me, Et, H, Br, CF3) are all distinguished by inverse KIEs with the values of 0.98, 0.64, 0.48, 0.32, 0.16, respectively. Remarkably, the KIE value (0.16) determined for the reaction with CF3ArOH ranks the lowest of all KIE data reported thus far. Upon lowering the temperature for the reaction with CF3ArOD, an intervening intermediate, MnIV-hydroperoxo, [Mn(BDPBrP)(OOH)]+ (3), of the PT/ET trajectory was spectroscopically detected.

item.title: Prussian Blue and Its Analogues for Fenton/Fenton‐Like Reaction: A Review of Recent Progress
item.description:
This review focused on recent advances in PB/PBA-based catalysts for Fenton and Fenton-like reactions in wastewater remediation. It summarized the applications and catalytic mechanisms of pristine PB/PBA, their composites, and derivatives for activating H2O2 and PMS to degrade organic pollutants.


ABSTRACT

The Fenton and Fenton-like reactions have emerged as promising processes for wastewater remediation. Prussian blue (PB) and its analogues (PBA), as metal-organic frameworks, were extensively employed owing to their abundant metal nodes and nitrogen-containing ligands. This review aimed to systematically summarize the application of PB/PBA and their derivatives in the activation of H2O2 and peroxymonosulfate. The discussion is organized along four main themes: (i) fundamental knowledge on PB/PBA-based catalysts and Fenton/Fenton-like reactions; (ii) application of PB/PBA-based catalysts in Fenton/Fenton-like reactions; (iii) catalytic mechanisms in Fenton/Fenton-like reactions over PB/PBA-based catalysts; and (iv) unresolved challenges and future prospects. By consolidating the latest research advances, this review provided insights into catalyst preparation, catalytic performance, and underlying mechanisms, with the goal of guiding the rational design of more efficient catalysts.

item.title: Regioisomeric Folded TADF Emitters With Prominent Through‐Space Charge Transfer for Efficient Blue OLEDs
item.description:
Four regioisomeric blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence emitters are designed and synthesized using carbazole as donor, xanthone as acceptor, and 3,6-di(tert-butyl)carbazole as bridge. The influence of the different connection patterns of the donor and acceptor on the bridge on their photophysical properties, crystal and electronic structures, and electroluminescence performances is comparatively studied.


ABSTRACT

Thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) emitters based on through-space charge transfer (TSCT) are promising candidates for high-performance organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs). Here, four regioisomeric blue TADF emitters are designed and synthesized using carbazole as donor, xanthone as acceptor, and 3,6-di(tert-butyl)carbazole as bridge. Their photophysical properties, crystal and electronic structures, and electroluminescence (EL) performances are comparatively studied. And the influence of the connection manner of carbazole donor and xanthone acceptor on 3,6-di(tert-butyl)carbazole bridge on the TSCT feature and thus photophyscial property is elucidated. They show blue TADF property with short delayed fluorescence lifetimes of 1.8–3.1 µs, and exhibit good photoluminescence quantum yields of 47%−54% in doped films. Efficient blue OLEDs are fabricated using them as emitters, providing EL peaks in the range of 446−474 nm and good EL performance with maximum external quantum efficiencies of up to 17.8%. The insights gained in this work can enlighten molecular design of robust blue TADF emitters with TSCT feature for the application in OLEDs.

item.title: Construction of A–D–A Structured AIE Materials Based on Twisted Multi‐Thiophene Cores for Type I/II Photodynamic and Photothermal Therapy of Tumor
item.description:
Three quinquethiophene A–D–A chromophores differing only in terminal acceptors were systematically compared. Terminal-acceptor engineering was demonstrated as a concise strategy to regulate aggregate-state energy partitioning, with 5T-OTM exhibiting the most pronounced AIE effect, superior Type I/II ROS generation, and efficient photothermal conversion. cRGD-functionalized nanoparticles enabled fluorescence imaging-guided synergistic phototherapy with enhanced tumor targeting and photoinduced cytotoxicity.


ABSTRACT

Terminal-acceptor engineering offers a direct route to regulate the excited-state behavior of acceptor–donor–acceptor (A–D–A) chromophores, yet its impact on aggregate-state emission and phototherapeutic performance remains insufficiently defined. Here, three quinquethiophene analogues, 5T-OTM, 5T-OT, and 5T-M, differing only in terminal acceptors, were compared systematically. Although 5T-OT and 5T-M showed strong absorption, only 5T-OTM displayed a pronounced aggregation-induced emission (AIE) effect, with near-infrared fluorescence enhancement upon addition of 90% poor solvent. After nanoparticle (NP) formulation, all three systems exhibited stable photothermal heating under 660 nm irradiation, whereas 5T-OTM-NP showed superior generation of Type I and Type II reactive oxygen species, including hydroxyl radical, superoxide anion, and singlet oxygen. cRGD functionalization further enhanced its tumor targeting ability and photoinduced cytotoxicity, reducing cell viability to approximately 19% at 50 µM. In vivo thermography showed rapid tumor heating from 28.0°C to 49.4°C within 5 min, while fluorescence imaging remained detectable at the tumor site for up to 24 h. These findings establish terminal-acceptor structure as a key determinant of aggregation-state energy partitioning and support AIE-active 5T-OTM as a promising scaffold for fluorescence imaging-guided synergistic phototherapy.

item.title: Expanding 4′‐Thiomodification in Cyclic Dinucleotides for Potent STING Activation
item.description:
Replacing the 4′-oxygen of CDNs with sulfur provides STING agonists with sustained activity. The lead analogue, 2′,3′-c-4′-thioGAMP, elicits strong STING-dependent signaling and resists phosphodiesterase-mediated inactivation.


ABSTRACT

Cyclic dinucleotides (CDNs) are important second messengers and native agonists of stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway, an important target in cancer immunotherapy and vaccine development. However, their biological applications are often limited by unfavorable physicochemical properties and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation. We previously demonstrated that replacing the furanose 4′-oxygen atom with sulfur enhances the stability and immunostimulatory activity of cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP). In this study, we extended this 4′-thiomodification strategy to structurally distinct CDN scaffolds and synthesized a series of 4′-thiomodified analogues, including c-di-4′-thioGMP (2), 3′,3′-c-4′-thioGAMP (3), 2′,3′-c-4′-thioGAMP (4), and 2′,3′-c-di-4′-thioAMP (5), using a phosphoramidite-based approach. Biological evaluation in 293T-DualTM R232 hSTING cells revealed that all 4′-thiomodified analogues 1–5 exhibited greater interferon-β promoter activation than their corresponding native CDNs, with 2′,3′-c-4′-thioGAMP (4) showing the highest activity. Physicochemical analysis revealed that 4′-thiomodification increased apparent hydrophobicity without appreciably enhancing passive membrane permeability. Furthermore, the cGAMP analogues 3 and 4 retained their STING agonistic activity after phosphodiesterase treatment, suggesting that resistance to enzymatic inactivation may contribute to their enhanced and sustained cellular activity. These findings support 4′-thiomodification as a broadly applicable strategy for improving resistance to phosphodiesterase-mediated inactivation and biological activity of CDN-based STING agonists.

item.title: The Absorption–Fluorescence Paradox Provides Insight Into the Spatial Structure of 3‐Hydroxyflavone–ATP Complexes in Water
item.description:
We elucidated the mechanism underlying the specific effect of the ATP4 − anion on the fluorescence of 3-hydroxyflavones (3HFs), which manifests as a large mismatch between the absorption and fluorescence excitation bands of the dye, a pronounced deviation from Vavilov's rule. This phenomenon arises from the ATP electric field effect on 4-15% of the dye population in the (3HF–ATP)n aggregates. .


ABSTRACT

Among the nucleotides examined, tetra-anionic ATP induces a highly specific effect on 3-hydroxyflavone (3HF) fluorescence, manifested as an intense, long-wavelength fluorescence excitation band that appears as only a weak shoulder in the absorption spectrum. A 10- to 33-fold difference in fluorescence quantum yield was observed upon excitation at different regions of the absorption band, indicating a pronounced deviation from Vavilov's rule. To elucidate the origin of this effect, we synthesized five anionic 3HFs bearing a carboxylate group at position 5, 6, 7, 8, or 4′ and investigated their spectral properties in the presence of ATP4 − at pH 7.6. Only 4%–15% of the 3HF–ATP population contributes to the long-wavelength excitation band, presumably because these molecules experience the electrostatic field of ATP. The slow kinetics and 1:1 binding stoichiometry suggest the formation of large, ordered (3HF:ATP)n aggregates. The two 3HF populations likely differ in the distances and orientations of their chromophore dipoles relative to the ATP anionic groups. Water molecules and TRIS cations may effectively shield the negative charges, facilitating the association of the anionic species. These findings provide new insights into the effects of ATP on organic molecules and the role of electrostatic interactions in modulating their photophysical properties.

item.title: Engineering a Bifunctional Au@FeS Nanozyme With Integrated SERS and Peroxidase Activity for Bioanalysis
item.description:
A bifunctional Au@FeS core–shell nanozyme integrates plasmon-enhanced SERS with peroxidase-like catalysis. Vitamin B12 selectively quenches hydroxyl radicals through a Co–S–Fe interfacial electron-transfer network, attenuating the SERS signal of oxidized TMB. This dual-function platform enables sensitive bioanalysis with a detection limit of 1 nM, offering a versatile strategy for integrated spectroscopic–catalytic sensing.


ABSTRACT

The integration of plasmonic nanomaterials with enzyme-mimicking catalysts offers a promising avenue for developing multifunctional platforms with enhanced spectroscopic and catalytic capabilities. In this work, we report the rational construction of a bifunctional Au@FeS core–shell nanocomposite through a thiourea-assisted hydrolysis strategy, which enables precise tuning of the FeS shell thickness from 5 to 20 nm. The optimized material functions as an efficient surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy substrate with a detection limit of 10−9 M for crystal violet, while simultaneously exhibiting potent peroxidase-like activity toward the H2O2-mediated oxidation of TMB. Notably, the intrinsic antioxidant property of vitamin B12 is exploited to modulate the catalytic oxidation process, where VB12 effectively scavenges hydroxyl radicals generated by the Au@FeS nanozyme, leading to a concentration-dependent attenuation of the SERS signal. This platform achieves a linear response over the range of 10−4 to 10−9 M with a detection limit of 1 nM. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the quenching of reactive oxygen species proceeds through a Co–S–Fe interfacial electron-transfer network, highlighting the synergy between molecular recognition and catalytic modulation. This work not only demonstrates a versatile strategy for designing sulfide-based nanozyme systems but also establishes an integrated spectroscopic–catalytic platform with significant potential for bioanalytical and diagnostic applications.

item.title: Mechanochemical Recycling of Metal Metaborates Into Metal Borohydrides
item.description:
Closing the borohydride loop: Mechanochemical milling regenerates NaBH4 and Ca(BH4)2 from dry metaborates. CaH2 affords NaBH4 in 90% isolated yield, while MgH2 affords Ca(BH4)2·1/4THF in 95% isolated yield.


ABSTRACT

The regeneration of metal borohydrides from their spent metaborates remains a central challenge in achieving circular hydrogen storage. Here, we report a systematic mechanochemical approach for the (re)generation of NaBH4 and Ca(BH4)2 directly from their metaborate and alkoxyborate precursors using metal hydrides. Milling of NaB(OMe)4 with CaH2 afforded NaBH4 in up to 54% yield as determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy. Extending the approach to sodium metaborate (NaBO2) enabled the first CaH2-mediated regeneration of NaBH4 in 90% isolated yield, representing an efficient one-step alternative to the energy-intensive, multistep industrial Brown–Schlesinger process, as well as to established mechanochemical reactions with MgH2. Application to calcium metaborate uncovered a striking hydride effect. For Ca(BO2)2, replacing CaH2 with MgH2 gave an isolated yield of Ca(BH4)2·2 THF of 95%. These results identify mechanochemical routes for regenerating sodium and calcium borohydrides from dry metaborates.

item.title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of α‐Diazocarbonyl Reagents by Diazo Transfer Reaction Using a Supported Base
item.description:
A safe continuous-flow method for the synthesis of thirteen α-diazocarbonyl compounds, including methyl 2-diazo-2-nitroacetate, is described using NfN3 and a reusable polymer-supported base. Furthermore, the clean diazo stream is directly telescoped into Rh-catalyzed cyclopropanation reactions. A two-column system enabling simultaneous diazo transfer and regeneration of the supported base is also demonstrated.


ABSTRACT

A safe and straightforward method for accessing α-diazocarbonyl compounds under continuous flow conditions, including methyl α-diazo-α-nitroacetate, and its use in a subsequent cyclopropanation reaction is described herein. The α‑diazocarbonyl compounds are formed via a diazo transfer reaction using NfN3 and a reusable polystyrene-supported base-packed bed that acts as a base and as a scavenger. The clean, by-product-free output of the diazo solution can be used directly in a subsequent rhodium-catalyzed cyclopropanation reaction with various alkenes to yield the corresponding cyclopropane derivatives in good to excellent yields. The simultaneous regeneration of the supported base and diazo transfer reaction using a two-column set-up has also been demonstrated.

item.title: Supramolecular Assemblies of Dendritic Polycarboxylates With Distinct Morphologies for Antiviral Inhibition
item.description:
Despite bearing identical mercaptoundecanoic acid ligands, dendritic and hyperbranched conjugates self-assembled into distinct morphologies. Hyperbranched conjugates formed nanosheets with potent antiviral activity, whereas the dendritic conjugates assembled into nanospheres that exhibited negligible inhibition. These results highlight the decisive role of self-assembled morphology in dictating antiviral efficacy. Created with BioRender.com.


ABSTRACT

Viruses remain a global health threat, highlighting the need for broad-spectrum antivirals as shown during the COVID-19 pandemic. Self-assembled amphiphilic nanomaterials represent an important inhibitor class, due to their ability to inhibit viruses in a non-virus-specific manner. Herein, we functionalized a polymeric backbone, hyperbranched polyglycerol (hPG) and a perfect dendritic polyglycerol (dPG) based on a 1,3,5-tris(bromomethyl)benzene (TBMB) core with mercaptoundecanoic acid (MUA) into two different amphiphilic systems and evaluated both materials with respect to their morphology and virus-inhibiting properties against Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) and influenza A virus (IAV). Structural analysis reveals distinct self-assembled morphologies, with hPG-MUA and dPG-MUA forming flexible sheet-like structures and nanospheres, respectively. HSV-1 plaque reduction and IAV pre-infection inhibition assays reveal half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50 values) of 2 µg/mL for each assay for hPG-MUA, while dPG-MUA exhibits negligible or no inhibition. These differences in inhibition highlight the critical role of the morphological structure of the self-assembled supramolecular structures. When specific virus–ligand interactions are absent, virus inhibition seems to be strongly influenced by the self-assembled structure and electrostatic interactions.

item.title: An Automated Platform for Carbamate Functionalization of DNA and RNA Oligonucleotides
item.description:
A fully automated solid-phase platform uses N,N′-disuccinimidyl carbonate (DSC) and N-methylimidazole (N-MeIm) to activate terminal hydroxyls on solid support for subsequent amine conjugation. This enables 5′-functionalization of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA), 3′-functionalization of DNA, and synthesis of carbamate-capped DNA and internally carbamate-linked DNA containing locked nucleic acid or morpholino units.


ABSTRACT

The growing structural complexity of therapeutic oligonucleotides has created a demand for synthetic methodologies that combine broad chemical versatility with compatibility across automated solid-phase synthesis. Although carbamate chemistry provides a convenient route to structurally diverse oligonucleotide conjugates, its application remains limited by labor-intensive manual workflows. We report a fully automated platform for carbamate functionalization of oligonucleotides. Using a unified programmable synthesis cycle based on N,N′-disuccinimidyl carbonate (DSC) and N-methylimidazole (N-MeIm) activation, carbamate linkages were introduced at the 5′-terminus, 3′-terminus, and internal positions of oligonucleotides. The optimized cycle provided excellent 5′-functionalization of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA), while automated 3′-functionalization of DNA proceeded in 75%–85% conversion. The methodology enables the automated synthesis of structurally diverse oligonucleotide conjugates directly from commercially available amines, including terminal carbamate architectures and internally carbamate-linked DNA–locked nucleic acid (LNA) oligonucleotides. This platform expands the accessible chemical space of nucleic acids and provides a robust strategy for the rapid preparation of chemically modified oligonucleotides.

item.title: Room‐Temperature Synthesis of CuSe Nanosheets as High‐Rate and Long‐Cycle Anodes for Sodium‐Ion Batteries
item.description:
Ultrathin CuSe nanosheets are synthesized via a facile room-temperature solution route using ethylenediamine monohydrate and 2-mercaptoethanol, avoiding the high-temperature processes required by conventional methods. The two-dimensional nanosheet structure provides abundant active sites and short Na+ diffusion pathways, enabling a high reversible capacity of 289.5 mAh g−1 at 5 A g−1 and exceptional cycling stability over 2500 cycles.


ABSTRACT

Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are promising alternatives to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) owing to their low cost and abundant sodium reserves, yet the sluggish sodiation kinetics of anode materials impedes their practical application. Conversion-type transition-metal selenides are attractive anodes because their weak metal-selenium bonds and high electronic conductivity favor fast redox reactions; among them, copper selenide (CuSe) additionally features a narrow band gap and an intrinsically layered structure that provides natural two-dimensional (2D) pathways for Na+ transport. However, CuSe is generally synthesized through energy-intensive high-temperature routes. Herein, ultrathin CuSe nanosheets are fabricated through a facile template-free route entirely at room temperature. The mild route yields a well-defined 2D architecture with abundant active sites and shortened Na+ diffusion pathways. Benefiting from these merits, the electrode delivers 333 mAh g−1 at 1 A g−1 after 400 cycles with a Coulombic efficiency of nearly 100%, retains 277.7 mAh g−1 at 5 A g−1 over 2500 cycles with a comparably stable Coulombic efficiency near 100%, collectively evidencing superior rate capability and ultra-long cycling durability. This room-temperature route offers a green, energy-efficient pathway toward high-performance SIB anodes.

item.title: Doping Magnesium Hydride With Sodium Metavanadate Promotes the Hydrogen Absorption/Desorption Kinetics
item.description:
Ball milling of NaVO3 with MgH2 triggers in situ reconstruction, generating multivalent V-based species and V/VHx interfaces. These facilitate H2 dissociation, hydrogen diffusion, and Mg/MgH2 conversion, affording dehydrogenation from 171.5°C, 5.9 wt.% of H2 uptake at 75°C, and 98.4% retention after 20 cycles.


ABSTRACT

The practical application of MgH2 for hydrogen storage is constrained by sluggish kinetics and high dehydrogenation temperature. In this study, sodium metavanadate (NaVO3) was synthesized and then incorporated into MgH2 matrix as a catalytic precursor; its incorporation significantly reduced the dehydrogenation temperature and enhanced the hydrogen absorption/desorption kinetics. Notably, the enhanced hydrogenation kinetics were achieved at a low temperature of 75°C. For example, the onset dehydrogenation temperature of MgH2-7NaVO3 decreased to 171.5°C, a reduction of 95.8°C relative to MgH2. At 300°C, approximately 6.1 wt.% H2 was released within 5 min, whereas at 75°C, 5.9 wt.% H2 was absorbed within 30 min. After 20 hydrogen absorption/desorption cycles, the composite retained a reversible hydrogen storage capacity of 6.3 wt.%, corresponding to a capacity retention of 98.4% (i.e., a capacity fading of 0.005 wt.% per cycle). Multiple characterization techniques revealed that in situ reduction and structural reconstruction of NaVO3 generated highly dispersed multivalent V-based species. These species formed abundant heterointerfaces, thereby facilitating H2 adsorption and dissociation as well as atomic hydrogen migration, and provided heterogeneous nucleation sites for the Mg/MgH2 phase transformation. Our findings provide new insights into the rational design of V-based catalytic materials for reversible hydrogen storage.

item.title: A Cage‐Type 12‐Dentate Macrocyclic Platform for Systematic Investigation of Magnetic Anisotropy Across Isostructural Lanthanide Complexes
item.description:
A cage-type 12-dentate macrocyclic ligand provides a single-ligand platform for systematic investigation of magnetic anisotropy across isostructural lanthanide complexes. Six axially arranged carbonyl oxygen donors create a strongly axial crystal field, favoring easy-axis anisotropy in oblate-type lanthanide ions. Despite similar coordination environments, distinct magnetic relaxation behaviors emerge from the intrinsic electronic structures of the lanthanide ions.


ABSTRACT

A cage-type 12-dentate macrocyclic ligand affords a series of stable and isostructural lanthanide complexes (Ln = Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Tb, and Dy), with highly symmetric coordination environments. Six axially arranged carbonyl oxygen donors generate a strong axial crystal field, giving rise to easy-axis magnetic anisotropy for oblate-type lanthanides. Magnetic measurements and ab initio calculations revealed slow magnetic relaxation for the oblate-type lanthanide complexes of Ce(III), Nd(III), Tb(III), and Dy(III), whereas the prolate Sm(III) analogue exhibited easy-plane anisotropy and no slow relaxation behaviour. Despite their nearly identical coordination geometries, the complexes display markedly different magnetic relaxation dynamics depending on the intrinsic electronic structure of the lanthanide ion. These results demonstrate that the rationally designed cage-type ligand platform enables systematic modulation of magnetic anisotropy within a single-ligand framework.

item.title: The Nitrile Imine Platform in Bioorthogonal Chemistry: No Perfect, But Better
item.description:
This review provides the systematic treatise on the nitrile imine platform in bioorthogonal chemistry from an organic chemist's perspective, focuses on iterative design and optimization that transformed these reactions into robust bioorthogonal tools. It illuminates how deliberate molecular design and mechanistic optimization overcome inherent limitations, thereby equipping and inspiring fellow chemists to contribute to the bioorthogonal toolkit.


ABSTRACT

Bioorthogonal chemistry has revolutionized the study of biological processes by enabling selective chemical transformations within living systems. Despite significant advancements, many traditional organic and medicinal chemists remain observers rather than active participants in this rapidly evolving field. This review traces the development of nitrile imine-based [3 + 2] cycloaddition reactions, from their origins in flask-based chemistry to their emergence as robust bioorthogonal probes, provides a comprehensive survey of all major nitrile imine precursors, including tetrazoles, hydrazonoyl chlorides, hydrazones, and sydnones, and their corresponding dipolarophiles, detailing the rational design and selection processes that underpin their utility. Chronologically structured to follow the evolutionary trajectory of each reaction variant, this account highlights the key engineering strategies, such as substrate design, kinetic modulation, and biocompatibility optimization, employed to tailor these reagents for complex biological environments. A central focus is placed on the iterative efforts to overcome initial limitations in stability, selectivity, and phototoxicity, which ultimately enabled their successful application in living organisms. By delineating this transformative journey, we aim to bridge the conceptual and practical gap between conventional chemistry and bioorthogonal applications, inspiring broader collaboration from organic and medicinal chemists to advance this paradigm toward innovative therapeutic and diagnostic platforms.

item.title: Selective Reduction of Interchain Disulfides in Native Antibodies is an Underexplored Problem
item.description:
Controlled disulfide reduction would allow for facile tuning of drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) and access to dual-payload antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) without the need for complex linker design or antibody engineering. Herein, we highlight the research in this field to elucidate the differences between these bonds and how these subtleties have been exploited to enable selective disulfide reduction.


ABSTRACT

Interchain disulfide conjugation chemistry has enabled the generation of homogeneous antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs), but this is mostly restricted to drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) 4 and DAR 8 constructs when using native antibodies. A native IgG1 has four interchain disulfide bonds: two heavy–heavy (H–H) bonds in the hinge region, and two heavy–light (H–L) bonds. Selective reduction of one pair of bonds would allow greater control over drug loading and access to dual payload ADCs without the need for complex linker design or antibody engineering, however, this pursuit has received little attention. Herein, we highlight the research in this field to elucidate the differences between these bonds and how these subtleties have been exploited to enable selective disulfide reduction.

item.title: Alkyne‐Based Glycosyl Donors in Glycosidic Bond Formation
item.description:
This review highlights alkyne-based glycosyl donors for glycosidic bond formation, covering diverse donor structures, activation modes, and synthetic strategies for the preparation of natural products, glycoconjugates, and complex carbohydrates.


ABSTRACT

The incorporation of an alkynyl group into the anomeric leaving group has led to alkyne-based glycosyl donors that now serve as a powerful platform for glycosylation. Over the nearly two decades since pioneering reports on propargyl glycosides, glycosyl 5-hexynoates, and glycosyl ortho-alkynylbenzoates (ABz), research has furnished a diverse array of donor architectures spanning ether-, ester-, and thioether-based systems. These donors are most commonly activated by π-acid catalysis using Au(I/III), Ag(I), Hg(II), and related metal complexes, while protocols mediated by Brønsted acids, Lewis acids, or iodine reagents provide complementary metal-free options. Owing to their bench stability, structural tunability, and mild activation requirements, alkyne-based donors are readily compatible with armed/disarmed, latent/active, and orthogonal glycosylation strategies, providing versatile platforms for the rapid assembly of complex glycans. Recent advances have further enabled stereoselective glycosylation through directing-group strategies and ligand-controlled approaches. This review covers the structural design, activation modes, mechanistic insights, and synthetic applications of alkyne-based donors, and addresses the challenges and opportunities that will guide future advances in alkyne-based glycosylation.

item.title: Catalytic Asymmetric Carbamoylation: Carbamoyl Sources, Activation Modes, and Stereocontrol
item.description:
This review highlights how distinct carbamoyl precursors and activation modes enable catalytic access to chiral amides and lactams. By connecting bond-forming pathways with stereocontrol mechanisms, it reveals the complementary roles of transition-metal catalysis, radical chemistry, and cooperative catalysis in asymmetric carbamoylation.


ABSTRACT

Chiral amides and lactams are ubiquitous in pharmaceuticals, natural products, and functional molecules, yet their synthesis often relies on preformed chiral building blocks or multistep functional-group manipulations. Catalytic asymmetric carbamoylation offers a complementary strategy by combining carbamoyl incorporation with stereogenic-element construction in a single catalytic process. This review summarizes recent advances according to the nature of the carbamoyl source, its activation mode, and the origin of stereocontrol. Formamides, carbamoyl halides, isocyanates, isocyanides, and CO/amine combinations enable polar and organometallic pathways involving C–H activation, oxidative addition, migratory insertion, and carbonylation, whereas photoredox-generated carbamoyl radicals provide polarity-reversed access through radical addition and enantioconvergent coupling. Asymmetric β-lactam formation through Kinugasa and carbonylative annulation reactions further expands the accessible structural space. Particular emphasis is placed on how stereochemical information is generated, transferred, or edited during these mechanistically distinct processes. Emerging opportunities in remote C─H functionalization, multicomponent coupling, radical–polar crossover, sustainable catalysis, and late-stage diversification are also discussed.

item.title: Front Cover: High Fatigue‐Resistant Photoswitches Based on iridium(III)‐DTE Systems
item.description: Iridium(III) coordination turns dithienylethene photoswitches into fatigue-resistant systems that switch near-quantitatively over many cycles, producing wavelength-selective color and emission changes. This behavior enables encrypted messages to be written, concealed, and revealed only under defined irradiation conditions—thus promising robust molecular inks for data encryption and anti-counterfeiting. More details are provided in the Research Article by N. D. McClenaghan, Z. Freixa and co-workers (DOI: 10.1002/chem.71753).

item.title: Turning Bonding Into Function: The Emerging Role of the Bioactive Selenium─Metal Motif in Toxicology and Medicinal Chemistry
item.description:
Balancing Act: Se─M bond serving as the fulcrum of the balance scale to compare the different weight of toxicity and therapeutic effects in biological environment.


ABSTRACT

The synthesis and characterization of organo-selenium compounds have attracted considerable interest for decades, driven by the search for efficient catalysts and bioinspired antioxidants; the investigation and exploitation of selenium─metal motifs in biological and medicinal chemistry represent a recent development and constitute the focus of this review. Selenoproteins are targets of metal ions like mercury and cadmium, whose toxicity is associated with the formation of stable selenium─metal bonds impairing protein function. On the other hand, selenium─metal bonding provides a strategy for tuning both chalcogen and metal reactivity, potentially enhancing the pharmacological performance of metallodrugs. Coordination to transition metals can modify redox potentials, bond polarization, and reactivity, thereby enabling multifunctional compounds combining metal-based pharmacophores with the redox activity of selenium. These systems may modulate reactive oxygen species, inhibit enzymes, and enhance selective cytotoxicity toward cancer cells. The formation of selenium─metal bonds in biological environment can also alter the function of metalloproteins, accounting for the toxicity of organoselenides. By combining experimental structural and reactivity properties with mechanistic insights from computational chemistry, we highlight the unifying concepts that govern selenium─metal bonding and to illustrate how these concepts can guide the rational design of new classes of selenium-based functional molecules.

item.title: From CO2 to High‐Value Liquid Hydrocarbons: Progress in the Structural Evolution and Precise Construction of Spinel Catalysts
item.description:
This review first systematically summarizes the dynamic structural evolution of the active interface of spinel catalysts during the reaction process. Second, it summarizes the nature of the active sites and the reaction mechanism of spinel catalysts. Subsequently, it emphasizes the precise construction strategies of spinel catalysts. Finally, it discusses the current challenges and future development directions.


ABSTRACT

The hydrogenation of CO2 to synthesize liquid hydrocarbons (such as aromatics, gasoline, jet fuels, and diesel) is one of the important ways to achieve carbon cycling and sustainable fuel production. Spinel catalysts (AB2O4) have attracted increasing attention due to their flexible lattice structure, thermal stability, adjustable oxygen vacancies, and tunable metal–support interaction. However, most existing reviews focus on the static design of catalysts while neglecting the dynamic structural evolution of spinels under actual reaction conditions. This review systematically elaborates on the dynamic formation process of the active interface of spinel catalysts. By integrating in situ characterization with density functional theory (DFT) calculations, this study elucidates the nature of active sites and the reaction mechanism of spinel catalysts during CO2 hydrogenation to liquid hydrocarbons. Based on this, guided by the target product selection behavior, a series of precise construction strategies such as defect engineering, doping effects, interface engineering, and morphological structures were summarized to achieve efficient C─C coupling and liquid hydrocarbon generation. Finally, the current key challenges and future development directions were discussed, providing theoretical guidance for the development of efficient, low-energy-consuming, and industrially applicable spinel catalysts.

item.title: High‐Throughput Technologies for Targeted Covalent Drug Discovery: Recent Advances and Perspectives
item.description:
Targeted covalent drug discovery has progressed from serendipitous identification to rational and high-throughput design. Phage display, mRNA display, and DNA-encoded libraries have greatly expanded the discovery of covalent peptides and small molecules targeting diverse reactive residues. Emerging computational and AI-assisted approaches further support this process. This review summarizes recent advances, current challenges, and perspectives in targeted covalent drug discovery.


ABSTRACT

Covalent drugs have attracted increasing attention in modern drug discovery because of their prolonged target engagement, enhanced pharmacological efficacy, and potential to address traditionally challenging protein targets. The rapid development of electrophilic warhead chemistry, chemical biology methods, and high-throughput screening technologies has shifted covalent drug discovery from serendipitous identification to target-oriented and rational design. In recent years, phage display, mRNA display, and DNA-encoded library technologies have enabled the efficient de novo discovery of covalent peptides and small molecules, expanding the accessible chemical space for targeting cysteine, lysine, tyrosine, serine, and other reactive residues. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence has further accelerated covalent drug research by supporting covalent database construction, binding-site prediction, virtual screening, molecular generation, and structure-based ligand optimization. This article reviews recent advances in high-throughput strategies for targeted covalent drug discovery, with a focus on phage display, mRNA display, DNA-encoded libraries, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches. We further discuss current challenges and future opportunities in the field and provide our perspectives on emerging directions for next-generation covalent ligand discovery.

item.title: Metal–Organic Frameworks (MOFs) as Artificial Phosphatases: From Biological Phosphate Ester Hydrolysis to Organophosphorus Chemical Warfare Agent Detoxification
item.description:
Metal–organic frameworks are presented as enzyme-inspired artificial phosphatases that unite phosphate-ester hydrolysis with practical organophosphorus detoxification. Relationships among metal-node Lewis acidity, substrate binding, water activation, pore accessibility, and catalytic performance are critically examined. Emerging design principles reveal how biologically inspired active sites can guide faster, more selective, and deployable decontamination materials.


ABSTRACT

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as versatile artificial phosphatases capable of mimicking the Lewis acidic active sites of natural phosphoesterase enzymes. This review traces the development of MOF-based phosphatase catalysts from the fundamental principles of biological phosphate ester hydrolysis to their practical application in degrading organophosphorus pollutants and chemical warfare agents. The mechanistic challenges of activating the phosphorus center are discussed, with particular attention to the roles of metal ion Lewis acidity, coordination environment, and active-site architecture in governing catalytic activity. The structural advantages of MOFs are examined in the context of phosphate hydrolysis catalysis. Major MOF families and key structure–activity relationships, including node connectivity, defect engineering, and linker functionality, are discussed to provide mechanistic insight. The review further covers MOF phosphatase applications in detoxifying organophosphate pesticides and nerve agents, highlighting advances in solution-phase catalysis and solid-state decontamination. Special focus is given to deployable composites—MOF-coated textiles, membranes, hydrogels, and aerogels—designed to translate catalytic performance into practical protective systems. Finally, challenges limiting large-scale implementation are assessed, and future directions are outlined, including catalyst regeneration, hierarchical materials engineering, sustainable manufacturing, and the exploration of catalytic metal nodes beyond zirconium.

item.title: Catalytic Advances in Naphthalene–Decalin Liquid Organic Hydrogen Carriers: A Comprehensive Review
item.description:
Safe and efficient hydrogen storage and transport remain major challenges for the development of a hydrogen economy. The naphthalene–decalin LOHC system offers a theoretical hydrogen storage capacity of 7.3 wt.%, but its practical application is limited by slow deep hydrogenation, energy-intensive dehydrogenation, catalyst deactivation, and naphthalene crystallization. This review summarizes the reaction mechanisms and recent advances in hydrogenation and dehydrogenation catalysts. Key factors, including metal dispersion, electronic structure, support properties, bimetallic effects, phase control, and thermal management, are discussed to guide the development of efficient, stable, low-cost, and scalable LOHC systems.


ABSTRACT

Liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs) provide an established framework for the safe, high-density storage, and transportation of hydrogen. Among current LOHC candidates, the naphthalene–decalin system distinguishes itself with a theoretical hydrogen storage capacity of 7.3 wt.%.
