Furthermore, all derivatives have been found to remain fluorescent in the solid-state (quantum yields of 7%–25%). The photophysical study is accompanied by single crystal x-ray structure analyses of representative compounds to establish the role of conformational geometry. Aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) can be (partially) suppressed and tuned via conformational control.

item.title: From a Dinitrogen‐Derived Hydrazido Complex to Inorganic Ammonium‐Type Cores Through Aluminum‐Promoted N─N Bond Cleavage
item.description:
An N2-derived chromium hydrazido complex is converted into inorganic ammonium-type cores within a three-component Cr/Si/Al system. AlMe3 promotes N─N homolysis through dual Lewis acid activation and subsequent Al─N bond formation, shifting N2 scission from simple nitride formation to multielement framework assembly.


ABSTRACT

N─N bond cleavage in molecular dinitrogen chemistry commonly leads to nitrido fragments. Here, we show that N─N scission can instead be coupled directly to multielement framework construction. Treatment of a side-on chromium bis(silyl)hydrazido complex with trimethylaluminum (AlMe3) induces N─N bond homolysis and assembles two inorganic ammonium-type cores in a CrN2Al2Si2 unit, wherein the central nitrogen atoms are coordinated by one chromium, two aluminum, and one silicon atom. Experiments and density functional theory support a pathway in which AlMe3 first removes the N-heterocyclic carbene ligand and then coordinates to both nitrogen atoms to weaken the N─N bond. N─N homolysis generates a radical intermediate that is trapped through Al─N bond formation coupled to the loss of two methyl radicals. Methane is detected among the headspace products. Thus, AlMe3 serves not simply as a Lewis acid but as an integral framework-forming reagent. This reaction converts N─N scission from simple nitride formation into multielement framework assembly and provides a distinct route from dinitrogen to inorganic ammonium-type cores.

item.title: Laser‐Triggered Covalent Patterning of Chirality‐Enriched (6,5)‐SWCNT Films With Chemically Distinct Radical Precursors
item.description:
Laser writing enables spatially controlled covalent functionalization of chirality-enriched (6,5)-single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) films. Three radical precursor classes produce distinct functionalization efficiencies and pattern definition. Raman mapping visualizes the written pathways, while wavelength-dependent and reference experiments reveal contributions from nanotube-mediated photoactivation and local heating.


ABSTRACT

The light-driven, spatially controlled covalent functionalization of single-walled carbon nanotube films requires control over precursor reactivity and irradiation conditions. In this study, chirality-enriched (6,5)-SWCNT films were coated with dibenzoyl peroxide, a diazonium salt, or a diaryliodonium salt and locally irradiated with a focused laser. The post-functionalization Raman mapping revealed an increase in the ID/IG+${{I}_D}/{{I}_{{{G}^ + }}}$ ratio along the laser-written pathways, which is consistent with the spatially confined covalent attachment of precursor-derived functional groups. The degree of functionalization and the spatial definition of the written patterns depended strongly on the precursor system. Laser-triggered covalent functionalization with an excitation wavelength of 457 and 532 nm yielded comparable functionalization-related Raman responses, whereas the response at 633 nm was weaker. This wavelength dependence shows that an exact E22 resonance excitation is not required and suggests that nanotube-mediated photoactivation and local heating may both contribute to the reaction. The patterned regions remained detectable after heating to 300°C. These results extend laser-triggered covalent patterning of (6,5)-SWCNT films to chemically distinct radical precursor classes.

item.title: Molecular Miniaturization of Carbon–Nitrogen‐Coupled Biphenylmethyl Radicals Enables Efficient Near‐Infrared Electroluminescence
item.description:
Molecular miniaturization with compact dimethylaminophenyl units resolves the trade-off between luminescence efficiency and processability in carbon–nitrogen-coupled BTM radicals. The synthesized DMA-PyID-BTM enables vacuum-deposited near-infrared OLEDs at 771 nm with an EQE of 2.7%, offering a practical design for high-performance radical emitters.


ABSTRACT

Stable luminescent radicals can enable efficient electroluminescence through spin-allowed doublet emission. In particular, carbon–nitrogen-coupled bis(2,4,6-trichlorophenyl)methyl (BTM) radicals have attracted attention as NIR emitters with tunable excited-state properties, and recent donor engineering has resulted in markedly enhanced photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs). However, bulky donors inevitably elevate molecular weights and sublimation temperatures, precluding vacuum thermal evaporation and device fabrication. Herein, we report a molecular miniaturization strategy to resolve this efficiency-processability trade-off. By replacing bulky donor moieties with compact 4-(N,N-dimethylamino)phenyl groups, two new carbon–nitrogen-coupled radicals, DMA-Cz-BTM and DMA-PyID-BTM, were designed and synthesized. Both radicals retain the favorable excited-state characteristics of donor-substituted BTM systems, including efficient donor–acceptor charge transfer, reduced excited-state structural relaxation, and suppressed nonradiative decay. Consequently, DMA-Cz-BTM and DMA-PyID-BTM exhibit near-infrared (NIR) emission at 756 and 776 nm with PLQYs of 24% and 21%, respectively. Importantly, the reduced molecular weight improves thermal processability and enables vacuum deposition of DMA-PyID-BTM for OLED fabrication. The resulting device achieves near-infrared electroluminescence at 771 nm with a maximum external quantum efficiency of 2.7%. This work establishes molecular miniaturization as an effective strategy to reconcile emission efficiency and device manufacturability, guiding the design of efficient radical emitters and radical OLEDs.

item.title: Defluoro–Dechloro Dearomative [5,5]‐Rearrangement–Diels–Alder Cascade Toward Naphthalene Construction
item.description:
We show that a cascade of dearomative [5,5]-rearrangement, Diels–Alder cyclization, and defluorinative/dechlorinative rearomatization assembles three distinct partners into polysubstituted naphthalenes.


ABSTRACT

In this study, we report a defluoronative–dechloronative synthesis of naphthalenes enabled by a sequential [5,5]-sigmatropic rear-rangement followed by a Diels–Alder reaction. The [5,5]-rearrangement of fluorinated aryl sulfoxides with β,γ-unsaturated nitriles forms highly unstable dearomatized sulfonium salts, which subsequently undergo Diels–Alder cycloaddition with chlorinated 1,3-diene derivatives. The resulting rearrangement–cycloaddition adducts then experience defluoronative–dechloronative rearomatization to furnish multisubstituted naphthalenes. The efficiency of this sequence depends on two factors: (1) fluorine on aryl sulfoxides ensures high regioselectivity of rearrangement and suppresses premature rearomatiza-tion; (2) chloride on the diene promotes the final aromatization to the desired structures. Moreover, each component of this three‑component process can be flexibly tuned, offering a modular strategy for accessing structurally diverse naphthalene derivatives.

item.title: Heteroatom‐Synergistic Modulation of Emission Bandwidth in Multi‐Resonance Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Molecules
item.description:
Heteroatom synergy modulates color purity by selectively regulating structural relaxation in two representative MR-TADF series. O→S replacement narrows the emission bandwidth in the B-centered series by restraining bond-length alterations, whereas it broadens the emission bandwidth in the N-centered series through more pronounced dihedral-angle alterations.


ABSTRACT

Multi-resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR-TADF) molecules are promising emitters for high-end displays offering narrowband emission with high color purity. This advantage is related to heteroatom-enabled resonance effects that reduce the reorganization energy, an effective descriptor of the full width at half-maximum (FWHM). Here, we elucidate the physicochemical origin of the color purity differences arising from heteroatom synergy in two representative MR-TADF series. In the B-centered MR-TADF molecules, the B-π-S analogues exhibit smaller FWHM (higher color purity) than the corresponding B-π-O analogues, owing to the decreased bond-length (BL) contribution to the reorganization energy. Conversely, in the N-centered MR-TADF molecules, the N-π-S analogues exhibit larger FWHM (lower color purity) than the corresponding N-π-O analogues, which is associated with the increased dihedral-angle (DA) contribution to the reorganization energy. Building on the above insights, we suggest two possible molecular-design approaches to enhance the color purity of MR-TADF molecules: (i) engineering the frontier-orbital distribution to suppress BL alterations; (ii) mitigating the orbital antibonding interaction to suppress DA alterations. To assess these approaches, four N-centered MR-TADF molecules were designed and computationally evaluated. The reductions in calculated reorganization energy and FWHM further support the proposed molecular-design approaches, highlighting their potential for improving the color purity of MR-TADF emitters.

item.title: Engineering Oxygen‐Vacancy‐Rich Cobalt‐Doped Alumina Washcoat on Monolithic Supports for Durable Peroxymonosulfate Activation via High‐Efficiency Singlet Oxygen Evolution
item.description:
This work presents a scalable monolithic catalyst (CAO@PAC) with oxygen-vacancy-rich Co-doped alumina washcoat on porous substrates. It activates PMS to generate 1O2 dominantly, achieving k = 0.218 min−1 for RhB removal and ultralow Co leaching (0.045 mg L−1). Oxygen vacancies enhance PMS adsorption and lower decomposition barriers. The catalyst sustains >20 cycles with easy recovery, offering a practical route for durable water treatment.


ABSTRACT

Singlet oxygen (1O2) is increasingly recognized as a key reactive species in advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) due to its long lifetime, wide pH tolerance, and selective oxidation behaviours toward electron‑rich organic contaminants. Nevertheless, rationally designing low-cost, durable, and easily recoverable catalysts for sustained high-yield 1O2 production remains challenging. Herein, we present a scalable method to fabricate a hierarchical monolithic catalyst (CAO@PAC) comprising an oxygen-vacancy-rich cobalt-doped alumina washcoat anchored on a porous substrate. The optimized CAO@PAC exhibited superior performance in activating peroxymonosulfate (PMS) for degrading rhodamine B (RhB) and other recalcitrant organic pollutants. Combined experimental and DFT studies revealed that oxygen vacancies at the Co─Al interface act as effective electron donors, enhancing PMS adsorption and lowering the energy barrier for its decomposition, thus promoting the dominant 1O2 generation pathway. Notably, the catalyst retained excellent structural integrity and catalytic activity over 20 consecutive cycles, with minimal cobalt leaching (0.026–0.077 mg L−1). Its monolithic porous architecture further facilitates mass transfer and enables easy recycling without post-treatment separation. This work establishes critical structure–property relationships in PMS activation and offers a practical route toward designing efficient, stable, and operationally simple catalytic oxidation systems for environmental remediation.

item.title: Engineering Axle Obstacles in Slide‐Ring Materials: From Molecular Stations to Programmable Mechanics
item.description:
Inspired by molecular stations, force-labile “speed bumps” along the polymer axle of SR networks convert continuous sliding into discrete, force-threshold energy dissipation. This arrest-and-release mechanism can enhance modulus, strength, extensibility, and toughness in mechanically interlocked polymers. This review summarizes recent progress in engineering axle obstacles for programmable mechanics and energy dissipation.


ABSTRACT

Slide-ring (SR) materials consist of cross-linked polyrotaxane macrocycles and show high toughness and fatigue resistance through the well-known “pulley effect”. Nevertheless, ring sliding within conventional SR networks proceeds in a continuous fashion, lacking intrinsic force thresholds, spatial programmability, and temporal control over energy-dissipation events. This review traces the conceptual evolution from stimulus-responsive molecular machines relying on molecular-scale “stations” for macrocycle shuttling toward the emerging paradigm of mechanically gated SR polymers. Along this line, it surveys the strategies developed by engineering obstacles along polymer axles, tracing a progression from geometric friction control and sacrificial dethreading to binding-site/threading-topology regulation and pushing-activated mechanochemistry, which collectively convert continuous sliding into discrete, force-programmed energy dissipation. Among these, force-labile “speed bumps” are highlighted as one emerging direction, in which pushing from a sliding macrocycle triggers mechanochemical cleavage and an “arrest-and-release” cycle. This strategy offers a modular platform for mechanically interlocked polymers with programmable mechanoresponses.
